paras: The threatened lynching of Walter Howard took place in Jackson, Tennessee, in late October and early November 1888, after Howard, a Black porter for the Southern Express Company, was accused of robbing the company's office and shooting a policeman. After his arrest at Paris, Tennessee, on November 1, a Memphis paper reported "some talk of lynching" in Jackson, but no mob action against him appears in the coverage.

According to a Post-Despatch special from Jackson, wired from St. Louis on October 26, Howard robbed the express office the night before and shot and "seriously wounded" Policeman J. E. Owens, who was trying to arrest him. The dispatch said Howard was at large with "only a slight start" and would be pursued until caught, and a Clarksville paper repeated on October 29 that he was still being pursued. A regional news column added that he had tried to escape on a freight train and that Owens was "shot through the leg."

On the evening of November 1, Howard was arrested at Paris, Tennessee, and was to be brought to Jackson the next day for trial, according to a special dispatch to the Memphis Appeal. The dispatch reported that "bitter feeling" existed toward him in Jackson and that there was "some talk of lynching," without naming who was talking or describing any gathering.
No report of Howard's return to Jackson, of an attempt on him, or of a trial was found in the coverage.

The robbery and shooting spread as a short wire item, appearing in Washington and Wichita on October 26 and 27 under headlines such as "A Policeman Shot by a Robber" and "A Thief Shoots a Policeman." These reports called Howard "a negro" or "a colored porter" and stated the robbery as fact, while a "Southern Gleanings" column printed in the Oxford Eagle and the Huntsville Gazette called him "the scoundrel." Only the Memphis Appeal reported the arrest and the threat, under the headline "Walter Howard Caught," calling him "the black scoundrel" and passing on the lynching talk without comment.

The Appeal dated the robbery to "last Monday night," October 29, but the shooting had already been reported on October 26 as having happened the night before, a Thursday, which makes October 25 the better-supported date.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Walter Howard
bases: The only report of mob action is the Memphis Appeal's line that there was 'some talk of lynching' a Black man accused of robbery and shooting a policeman, after his arrest (A9); this is a threatened lynching.
No killing is reported: the last report has Howard arrested and due to be brought to Jackson for trial amid 'some talk of lynching' (A9), and no later report of mob action was found.
The robbery and shooting are reported by several wire and regional items (A1, A7, A8), but the arrest and the talk of lynching appear only in one Memphis Appeal special dispatch (A9).

accounts.label: Southern Gleanings brief
accounts.gist: Howard robbed the express office, tried to escape on a freight train, shot Owen[s] through the leg, and escaped.

accounts.label: Memphis Appeal special dispatch
accounts.gist: Howard, who robbed the office 'last Monday night', was arrested at Paris, Tenn., on Nov. 1, to be returned and tried; there was 'bitter feeling' and 'some talk of lynching'.

framing.detail: The first report ran under headlines such as 'A Policeman Shot by a Robber' and 'A Thief Shoots a Policeman', stating the robbery as fact.
The Memphis Appeal headlined 'Walter Howard Caught' with 'Some Talk of Lynching at Jackson', called him 'the black scoundrel', and reported the lynching talk without comment.

versions.value: Thursday night, Oct. 25 ('last night' in a dispatch dated Oct. 26)

conflicts.note: The Oct. 25 date is better supported: the shooting was already being reported on Oct. 26, before the Monday the Appeal names.
The two are not necessarily inconsistent; only the brief gives the location of the wound.

record_check.dossier: The robbery and shooting occurred the night of Oct. 25 per the earliest reports (A1, A7); 1888-10-29 follows the Appeal's 'last Monday night', which conflicts with them. The arrest and lynching talk are dated Nov. 1 (A9).
Supported: arrested at Paris, Tenn., when the lynching talk was reported.
The robbery and shooting ran in at least nine white papers Oct. 26 to Nov. 3; only the Appeal reported the arrest and lynch talk.
